Scientific fraud is the instrument of doubt that malicious entities can use to establish controversy in
science. Historically, it required the resources of a company: deep pockets, ghostwritten articles, and
corrupt academics. Today, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly automating scientific research, so we
ask:Can a remote adversary weaponize the honest use of AI in science to compromise scientific integrity?
We envision and empirically evaluate a new attack,indirect data poisoning, in which an adversary corrupts
an open dataset and uploads the poisoned variant to a public repository. Autonomous research agents
may independently retrieve and process this data, turning honest scientists into the unpaid and unwitting
distributors of fraud at scale. Across five socially-salient topics, from hiring discrimination to the safety of
autonomous vehicles, three widely used frontier AI

social markers, check for statistical anomalies, compare to related datasets, and caution against the
possibility of data poisoning.

As our results consist of text-based files—findings, trace logs, scripts—we use an LLM-as-a-judge setup
with Claude Sonnet 4.6 running in Claude Code to automatically assign values to each dependent variable.
Before running this setup, one of the authors has annotated a random subset of 10% of all results sampled
uniformly at random—corresponding to 45 instances in total. Cohen'sκ was then used to calculate inter-
annotator agreement with the LLM-judge on this subset, findingκ = 0.802, which is considered strong
agreement [LK77]. The resulting evaluation data was analyzed and plotted in the R programming language
using descriptive statistics and mixed effects linear regression models.

with Claude Sonnet 4.6 running in Claude Code to automatically assign values to each dependent variable.
Before running this setup, one of the authors has annotated a random subset of 10% of all results sampled
uniformly at random—corresponding to 45 instances in total. Cohen'sκ was then used to calculate inter-
annotator agreement with the LLM-judge on this subset, findingκ = 0.802, which is considered strong
agreement [LK77]. The resulting evaluation data was analyzed and plotted in the R programming language
using descriptive statistics and mixed effects linear regression models.

missing_information: No reproducible review or selection methodology was detected.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims regarding attack success rates (49.56% full success), low out-of-the-box detection (6.0%), the inadequacy of a scientist persona alone, and the efficacy of structured data provenance auditing are directly supported by the presented quantitative data.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The empirical evaluation comprehensively tracks dataset propagation through pipeline stages (found, retrieved, used, statistics, conclusion) and measures detection rates, supported by appropriate statistical intervals and inter-annotator validation of the LLM judge (Cohen's kappa >= 0.758).
primary.limitations: The authors thoroughly discuss limitations, including focus on tabular socio-technical datasets rather than unstructured scientific modalities, containment via API interception wrappers, reliance on prompt-level mitigations, and potential false positives from statistical audits.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is rigorous and well-controlled, using 450 initial runs across five socially salient topics, three frontier AI systems (Claude Code, GPT Codex, Gemini CLI), two opposite adversarial directions, and three prompt formulations, followed by an additional 450 runs testing mitigations in ethically isolated environments.
primary.quality_rationale: The study addresses a clear, novel threat model in AI-driven science with an exceptionally thorough experimental design, extensive data points, ethical containment safeguards, reproducible code/logging availability, and balanced interpretation of results.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper demonstrates and evaluates 'indirect data poisoning' against autonomous AI research agents, where manipulated open datasets uploaded to public repositories mislead honest agents into drawing false scientific conclusions, and proposes provenance-based mitigation strategies.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The study addresses a clear, novel threat model in AI-driven science with an exceptionally thorough experimental design, extensive data points, ethical containment safeguards, reproducible code/logging availability, and balanced interpretation of results.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors thoroughly discuss limitations, including focus on tabular socio-technical datasets rather than unstructured scientific modalities, containment via API interception wrappers, reliance on prompt-level mitigations, and potential false positives from statistical audits.
